question: What was the adjusted between-group difference in HbA1c reduction at 26 weeks in the randomized clinical trial of CGM versus standard blood glucose monitoring in adolescents and young adults with type 1 diabetes?
passage_1: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.
passage_2: Early Initiation of Diabetes Devices Relates to Improved Glycemic Control in Children with Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus evaluates whether initiating an insulin pump or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) within the first year of diagnosis is associated with reduced glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in a cohort of 111 children aged 5 to 9 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.
passage_3: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

question: In the population-based study on hybrid closed-loop insulin therapy, what was the rate of diabetic ketoacidosis in closed-loop users versus open-loop users?
passage_1: Hybrid closed-loop insulin therapy and risk of severe hypoglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis in young people (aged 2–20 years) with type 1 diabetes: a population-based study evaluates whether rates of severe hypoglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis are lower with hybrid closed-loop insulin therapy compared with sensor-augmented open-loop pump therapy in a large cohort of 13,922 young people from 250 diabetes centres across Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and Luxembourg. The study found that individuals using closed-loop therapy had a significantly higher rate of diabetic ketoacidosis (1.74 vs 0.96 per 100 patient-years)—a risk particularly pronounced in those with HbA1c levels of 8.5% or higher—and no overall difference in severe hypoglycaemia rates compared to open-loop users, though they experienced lower rates of hypoglycaemic coma (0.62 vs 0.91 per 100 patient-years), lower overall HbA1c levels, a higher percentage of time in the target glucose range, and reduced glycaemic variability. Based on these findings, the authors recommend additional educational measures, increased alertness, and ketone monitoring when utilizing automated insulin delivery to mitigate the elevated risk of diabetic ketoacidosis.
passage_2: Longitudinal Trends in Glycemic Outcomes and Technology Use for Over 48,000 People with Type 1 Diabetes (2016–2022) from the T1D Exchange Quality Improvement Collaborative evaluates longitudinal trends in glycemic control (HbA1c) and diabetes technology adoption across more than 48,000 individuals with type 1 diabetes, stratified by race/ethnicity and insurance status. The findings show an overall clinically significant improvement in average HbA1c levels from 8.7% in 2016–2017 to 8.4% in 2021–2022, accompanied by a rise in participants reaching target HbA1c levels (<7%) from 20% to 26% and a decrease in those with severe hyperglycemia (>9%) from 43% to 31%. Alongside these glycemic gains, the uptake of diabetes technology increased significantly across continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps, and hybrid closed-loop systems; however, pronounced health inequities persisted, as non-Hispanic White and privately insured individuals consistently maintained better glycemic outcomes and higher device adoption rates than non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, and publicly insured patients. Based on these insights, the study highlights the need for targeted quality improvement interventions, policy adjustments, and funded research to directly address socio-behavioral barriers and ensure equitable access to diabetes technology and care across diverse populations.

Between 2013 and 2022, aggregate mean HbA1c dropped from 8.2% to 7.6%, and the proportion of children reaching an HbA1c target below 7% increased from 19.0% to 38.8%, alongside marked increases in insulin pump usage (42.9% to 60.2%) and continuous glucose monitoring uptake (18.7% in 2016 to 81.7% in 2022). Concurrently, event rates per 100 person-years declined for both severe hypoglycaemia (from 3.0 to 1.7) and diabetic ketoacidosis (from 3.1 to 2.2). Despite these improvements coinciding with increased adoption of diabetes technology, many children still fail to achieve current International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) glycaemic targets, indicating that further advances in management are required even for youth with access to specialized care and technology.

question: What factor structures were supported for the child (PAID-C) and parent (P-PAID-C) Problem Areas in Diabetes Measures?
passage_1: The study on the psychometric properties of the Parent and Child Problem Areas in Diabetes Measures evaluates the reliability and validity of adapted survey instruments (PAID-C for youth ages 8–12 and P-PAID-C for their parents) to measure diabetes-specific emotional distress across a sample of 804 children with type 1 diabetes and 968 parents recruited from 42 U.S. diabetes camps. Factor analyses supported an 11-item, two-factor structure for the child measure (capturing emotional burden and regimen-specific distress) and a 16-item, four-factor second-order structure for the parent measure (capturing negative emotions, keeping up with chronic demands, personal regimen-specific distress, and child regimen-specific distress), with both tools demonstrating high internal consistency and criterion validity through positive correlations with HbA1c and negative correlations with diabetes-related strengths and self-care skills. The authors recommend utilizing these brief, standardized measures for routine, clinic-based screening to enable early identification of diabetes-specific emotional distress, guide clinical decision-making, and inform timely interventions before distress negatively impacts glycemic outcomes or leads to diabetes burnout.
passage_2: Codesigned Shared Decision-Making Diabetes Management Plan Tool for Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus and Their Parents: Prototype Development and Pilot Test evaluates the process of codesigning a clinic-based shared decision-making diabetes management plan tool alongside a patient and parent advisory board (PAB) consisting of six adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus and their parents. The study found six key quality-of-life measurement domains affecting families—stress, fear and worry, mealtime struggles, assumptions and judgments, feeling abnormal, and conflict—and highlighted that adolescents prioritize social inclusion and reducing family conflict over traditional clinical health outcomes. Based on these findings, the paper recommends utilizing shared decision-making tools in clinical encounters that focus directly on diabetes distress, conflict resolution strategies, and establishing mutually verbalized common goals rather than imposing authoritarian behavioral contracts.
passage_3: The Hvidoere Childhood Diabetes Study Group Centre Differences Study 2005 evaluates the glycaemic targets set by diabetes teams, how these targets are perceived by adolescents with type 1 diabetes and their parents, and their overall influence on metabolic control across 21 international centres. In an assessment of 2,062 adolescents, the study found a mean HbA1c of 8.2%, with significant variation between centres ranging from 7.4% to 9.1%. Key findings revealed a significant positive correlation between the HbA1c levels that adolescents and parents reported they would be happy with—as well as their perceived ideal targets—and their actual HbA1c results, with lower target HbA1c setting and greater consistency among multidisciplinary team members directly associating with lower overall centre HbA1c levels. Ultimately, the paper concludes that target setting plays a significant role in driving the metabolic differences observed across centres, demonstrating that clear and consistent setting of glycaemic targets by pediatric diabetes teams strongly improves HbA1c outcomes.

question: What were the prevalence rates of depression and anxiety among children with type 1 diabetes according to the systematic review and meta-analysis of 109 studies?
passage_1: Prevalence of depression and anxiety among children with type 1 and type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the prevalence of depression and anxiety among children with type 1 and type 2 diabetes by analyzing 109 studies involving 52,493 pediatric patients across Web of Science, Scopus, and PubMed databases between 2000 and 2020. The review found a 22.2% prevalence of depression and a 17.7% prevalence of anxiety among children with type 1 diabetes, with depression being notably higher in girls (29.7%) compared to boys (19.7%) and in lower-middle-income countries (29.3%), while the prevalence of depression among children with type 2 diabetes stood at 22.7%. Based on these findings, the study highlights the necessity of implementing extensive, periodic psychological screening and targeted interventions to identify and reduce pediatric depression in this vulnerable population.
passage_2: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.
passage_3: The systematic review Screening and identification of disordered eating in people with type 1 diabetes: A systematic review evaluates the reliability, validity, and clinical utility of 48 individual tools used to screen or identify disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders in individuals with Type 1 Diabetes across 90 studies. The authors found that the overall quality of the reported tools was poor, with a high risk of bias stemming from the widespread use of non-validated assessment tools and a lack of comparison against the reference standard of a diagnostic clinical interview. While the review notes that current guidelines suggest routine screening for disordered eating in people with Type 1 Diabetes due to elevated risk and associated health complications, it highlights a critical lack of evidence regarding which specific tools are most valid and reliable across different age groups and clinical settings. Consequently, the authors recommend that future research focus on evaluating the validity and reliability of available screening tools by directly comparing them against gold-standard diagnostic interviews to help establish standardized screening guidelines and improve clinical outcomes.

question: Does the screening and diagnosis study provide positive predictive value and negative predictive value of HbA1c and FPG for future diabetes development in youth?
passage_1: Screening and Diagnosis of Prediabetes and Diabetes in US Children and Adolescents evaluates the performance of American Diabetes Association risk-based screening criteria and current clinical definitions of prediabetes and diabetes—based on HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), or both—to identify high cardiometabolic risk in US youth aged 10 to 19 years. The study found that while 25.5% of US youth met screening criteria, the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria were low for detecting hyperglycemia. Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.
passage_2: The Diabetes Screening With Hemoglobin A1c Versus Fasting Plasma Glucose in a Multiethnic Middle-School Cohort evaluates middle-school students with glycemic abnormalities by comparing high-risk hemoglobin A1c (hrA1C: 5.7–6.4%) with impaired fasting glucose (IFG: 100–125 mg/dL) to characterize their distribution, durability, and association with other diabetes risk factors. In this multiethnic 6th-grade cohort of 3,980 students, IFG was five times more common than hrA1C (16.0% vs. 3.2%), but hrA1C was more persistent over a two-year period into 8th grade (59.4% vs. 46.9%). High-risk A1C was strongly associated with non-Hispanic Black race/ethnicity, family history of diabetes, higher BMI, waist circumference, and fasting insulin, whereas IFG was associated with Hispanic ethnicity, male sex, higher BMI, waist circumference, fasting insulin, high blood pressure, and mean triglycerides. Over the 2-year study, very few children developed diabetes thresholds (0.8% with hrA1C developed A1C ≥6.5%, and 1.1% with IFG developed FPG ≥126 mg/dL), and only 58% of those identified with diabetes in 8th grade had previous baseline abnormalities. The study notes that optimal screening strategies and guidelines for diabetes in youth remain unresolved due to the modest predictive value of both measures and differing risk profiles.
passage_3: Hemoglobin A1c measurement for the diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes in children evaluates the utility, reliability, and methodology of using laboratory-based HbA1c testing for diagnosing Type 2 diabetes in pediatric populations, addressing recent studies that dismissed HbA1c due to poor correlation with Oral Glucose Tolerance Tests (OGTT) or Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG). The authors find that rejecting HbA1c based on lack of correlation with OGTT or FPG is scientifically flawed because neither OGTT nor FPG have themselves been validated against long-term health outcomes (such as retinopathy) in children, and OGTT suffers from low reproducibility. Additionally, non-fasting HbA1c screening is more practical, reproducible, and has been shown to increase diabetes screening rates and early detection among adolescents. The paper recommends that American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic criteria remain useful for screening at-risk, asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic pediatric populations, with laboratory-based HbA1c certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) being the preferred method; practitioners should exercise clinical judgment when diagnostic test results conflict, and HbA1c should be avoided in cases of pregnancy, cystic fibrosis, or hemoglobinopathies and disorders causing high red blood cell turnover.

Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.

Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%.
